one_liner: Node.js runtime fusing RocksDB-backed tables, app code and MQTT/WebSocket pub/sub; vendor benchmark: lower latency than Kafka stacks at ≤1k events/s.
what_it_does: Harper (formerly HarperDB) runs a database, record cache, application server and message broker in one Node.js process. You declare tables in a GraphQL schema (`@table`, `@export`), get REST endpoints generated, add custom `Resource` classes in JavaScript, and publish or subscribe to table and topic changes over MQTT 3.1.1/5, WebSockets or SSE, with replay from the table's audit log and durable MQTT sessions. It is not a Kafka replacement at the API level: there is no Kafka wire protocol, so producers, consumers and stream jobs have to be rewritten against Harper's resources and protocols. The Apache-2.0 core runs on one node. The 3-node replication used in the benchmark comes from Harper Pro, which is under Elastic-2.0.
how_it_is_fast: The speedup comes from removing hops. The durable write, the enrichment lookups and the downstream notify all run in one process against embedded RocksDB (the `@harperfast/rocksdb-js` native binding; LMDB is the legacy engine), with a WeakRef-based LRU record cache, so there is no network or serialization step between database, cache and broker. Subscribers are fed from the audit (transaction) log: each 'committed' event schedules one `setImmediate` pass that walks the log and dispatches to per-key subscriber maps on every worker thread. Bursts collapse into one pass, and a QoS 0 MQTT frame is encoded once and shared by all matching subscribers. In the benchmark, the conventional stack pays for Debezium's WAL polling (the authors estimate 100-300 ms, not measured) and for a 50 ms Kafka consumer batch window, and Harper's MQTT path has neither.
when_to_use: Write-then-notify or filtered fan-out at tens to about 1,000 events/s, where you would otherwise wire up Postgres + Debezium + Kafka + Redis. The benchmark measured 9.4 ms vs 523 ms p50 at 50 events/s and 12.5 ms vs 165 ms at 10 events/s.
Pushing live state to browsers or devices over MQTT or WebSockets when the consumer needs the latest value per key, not every intermediate change.
Live dashboards with windowed aggregates at low per-key event rates, where Kafka Streams' suppress-until-window-close holds back results (W3 freshness: 1.05 s vs 3.65 s p50, 1.56 s vs 13.6 s p95).
Node.js teams that want the database, API and pub/sub in one deployable unit, and that accept Harper Pro (Elastic-2.0) or Harper Fabric for multi-node.
when_not_to_use: Throughput-bound log ingestion at 10^5-10^6 events/s. The benchmark never ran a steady state above about 1,000 events/s, and its authors expect Kafka to win or tie on real multi-node hardware.

CDC, event sourcing or audit consumers that need every change. Record subscriptions over in-process subscribe(), SSE and MQTT coalesce intermediate updates under burst writes, dropping up to 88.5% at threads: 4, with no gap marker (harper#2483, open).
Point reads against live aggregates. Kafka Streams Interactive Queries answered in 2.75 ms p50 vs Harper's 17 ms through a REST endpoint.
Stacks that depend on Kafka clients, Connect, Streams or Schema Registry, because Harper does not speak the Kafka protocol.
When you need OSI-licensed multi-node replication. Replication ships in Harper Pro under Elastic-2.0, which forbids offering it as a hosted or managed service.

integration.form: module: npm package `harper` with a CLI (`npm i -g harper`) or a Docker image; it is a server runtime with native addons, not an embeddable library
integration.dependencies: About 70 npm dependencies, including the native addons @harperfast/rocksdb-js, lmdb and argon2, plus fastify, msgpackr, cbor-x, ws and mqtt-packet. Optional: uWebSockets.js (glibc only, no musl) and the HNSW/fulltext addons. Multi-node replication needs Harper Pro.
integration.min_toolchain: Node.js ^22.18.0 or >=24 (package.json engines). There is a Bun integration-test target, but Node is the primary runtime.
integration.platforms: The Harper Pro README says it is tested on Linux amd64/arm64, macOS Intel/Apple Silicon and Windows. The core's Windows CI gate runs only a subset of the unit tests.
integration.thread_safety: Each node runs several worker threads, and application modules load once per thread, so module-level side effects and subscriptions run N times. Record writes are RocksDB transactions with conflict retries. Cross-node writes resolve last-writer-wins by timestamp. table.lock() excludes only other lock() callers, and only on a single node (Phase 0).
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: false: there is no Kafka wire protocol or client API, so producers and consumers must be rewritten for MQTT/WebSocket/SSE/REST or Harper Resource classes

gotchas: In the benchmark's Harper handlers, async work fired after the handler returned was cancelled (most fire-and-forget notifies were dropped). The harness therefore awaits an outbound HTTP notify inside the request. That notify is logged on failure and never retried, unlike the durable Debezium-to-Kafka path it is compared against.

Resource modules load once per worker thread. A table.subscribe-based notifier fired about 7 times per node (21 times across 3 nodes), and W3 window-close notifies fired 2-21 times. At benchmark time there was no leader-election or compare-and-swap primitive to deduplicate them.

Durability comparable to Kafka's acks=all must be opted into per request with `this.getContext().replicatedConfirmation = N`, where N counts peers. The default is async replication, and the MQTT broker has no per-write confirmation.

Several subscription bugs are open: ending a subscription during fan-out makes the next subscriber miss that event (#2771), deletes are reported as empty puts or bare nulls (#2738, #2438), and startTime replay drops events committed after the audit cursor ends (#2311).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Choose Harper over standalone brokers such as NATS JetStream, RabbitMQ or Mosquitto when the broker would otherwise sit beside a separate database and cache, and your app logic can run as Node.js inside the same process. Choose Redpanda or AutoMQ instead when you need Kafka API compatibility and Kafka-scale throughput.
verified_claims_summary: This is a Harper-affiliated whole-stack benchmark run in one OrbStack VM on an Apple Silicon Mac (24 GB, 8 vCPU; chip not stated). It pits a 3-node Harper Pro cluster (digest-pinned image, RocksDB default) against 3 Kafka brokers at RF=3 plus Postgres/Debezium/Redis/Kafka Streams as each workload needs. Harper's p50 was 9.4 ms vs 876 ms with Go glue, or 523 ms with language-matched Node glue, which the authors' own decision log adopts as the headline (~56x, not ~100x); 12.5 ms vs 165 ms on W2; 1.05 s vs 3.65 s on W3 freshness; and 1.4 ms vs 57 ms on W4 at 1,000 events/s, while Kafka Streams won point lookups (2.75 ms vs 17 ms). The runs were short (15-30 s at 10-1,000 events/s, 3 paired runs, one run per stack for W3), W1 delivered only 83-84% on both stacks although the README says 100%, and a containerized Harper W4 variant cut the W4 gap to about 10-20x.
status_note: The core is under active development: v5.2.14 and v5.3.0-beta.3 were released 2026-09-25, and the repo has 941 open issues and 90 stars. The core is Apache-2.0, but the replication behind the benchmarked 3-node setup is Elastic-2.0 Harper Pro, and the benchmark repo is a 0-star snapshot created and last pushed on 2026-05-28.
